The forest question is very interesting, I will reflect on this. My immediate thoughts are... Plants can communicate with each other via airborne hormones, but I doubt it is sufficient to propagate a meaningful signal, and it is too dependent on external factors. There is also indirect communication (e.g. plants can sense their environment through photoreceptors etc.), so perhaps the collective actions of the forest could be interpreted as some sort of Game-of-Life-like emergent intelligence (I think you'd be stretching the word to say this was 'consciousness' though). I don't think we really have a proper notion of what conciousness is yet. We have a tendancy to start with the basic assumption that other animals are different, and be surprised when we find evidence for similarities. For example, there's some basic aspects of the way out brain pays attention to things that are also found in bumblebees.

I don't see a fundamental reason why we're not just a more complex neural network and it's all just a sliding scale based on connectivity of neurons and the complexity of structure in the brain.

What is interesting is that Elephants have a brain that is much larger than humans, but we can't really see evidence that they are 'smarter' than we are, in any way that we can measure. Whales can have even larger brains. Conversely, crows have much smaller brains, but can still use tools and perform complex problem solving.

The trouble with suggesting that everything is just a neural network of varying levels of sophistication, is that it makes things a bit murky, ethically. If it's a sliding scale, do we base what animals it's ok to eat or experiment on on their neural complexity? Even though there may not be a fundamental cut and dried difference? There's the scene from futurama when they're eating the dolphin, and Farnsworth asks for the speech centre of the brain.

And if not that, are we just basing it on what they can physically do? A cow can't build an abbatoir, so it just loses. Or maybe it's just tradition. We've always done it that way, and that's how we work, as omnivores in the natural order, so we should just carry on.

As far as forests go, there are maybe better examples, but I suppose you might be thinking of lots of individuals making a more complex whole, like we have so many individual cells that make up a person. There is also a suggestion that plants can signal each other, but it lacks the feedback loop that is the fundamental root of all cognition, so it can never develop any conciousness.
